_about: Real numbers for the landing, power and comms flight traits (traits/landing.js, wave 5). Keyed by part id and kit option id; each number names its source in `sources` (by id). 'estimate' marks a number nobody publishes for this exact case: it is a defensible choice, said so. Game scaling is written out under `gameScale`. neutral: the traits with no data (the flight as before).

gameScale.legsDesignMass: The game's ships land at 8 to 35 t, so each leg set's design mass is set for that class (estimate); the design speed and stroke are the real hardware's.
gameScale.surfaceTimeWhy: A Mars EVA runs about 87 times faster than real time: the suit's 7.3 hours of walking on one fill last 300 s (src/surface/oxygen.js, traits/life.json). Stored energy on the surface (the rover batteries, the ship's batteries and fuel-cell reactants) is divided by 87, so it runs out and refills on the same clock as the oxygen; powers (W) and the driving energy per metre stay real, so a rover's range is 87 times shorter than the real machine's.
gameScale.upload: A real upload takes from an hour (relay smallsat: its next pass, then a minute of data) through about three hours (dish: Earth must be up) to weeks (omni antenna). The wait in the game grows with the logarithm of the real time: 3 s for anything under a minute, plus 6 s for every ten times longer, at most 60 s. The relay counts the hop the crew waits for (surface to orbiter); its own slow link home (about 8 kbit/s, MarCO-class) forwards the data over the following hours.
gameScale.chuteLoad: Real Mars chutes open at about 10 km where the dynamic pressure is 0.6 to 0.9 kPa. On this 1/10-size Mars the chutes open lower, at up to 2.5 kPa, which a real disk-gap-band is not rated for. The game counts only the Mach limit of each canopy type; the opening load is not modelled.

touchdown.en: Touched down at {value} m/s ({vVert} m/s down, {vHoriz} m/s sideways); at {massT} t these legs take {limit} m/s.
touchdown.vi: Chạm đất ở {value} m/s ({vVert} m/s thẳng đứng, {vHoriz} m/s ngang); với {massT} tấn, bộ chân này chịu được {limit} m/s.

whatIfFail.en: With {alt} instead of {mine}, the legs would take only {altLimit} m/s: this touchdown would have broken them.
whatIfFail.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine}, chân chỉ chịu {altLimit} m/s: cú chạm đất này đã làm gãy chân.

whatIfPass.en: With {alt} instead of {mine}, the legs would take {altLimit} m/s and this {value} m/s touchdown would have held.
whatIfPass.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine}, chân chịu được {altLimit} m/s và cú chạm đất {value} m/s này đã an toàn.

tipOver.en: Sideways at {value} m/s on a {spanM} m stance: a ship this tall tips over above {limit} m/s.
tipOver.vi: Trôi ngang {value} m/s trên thế đứng rộng {spanM} m: tàu cao thế này sẽ đổ khi vượt {limit} m/s.

whatIfFail.en: With {alt} instead of {mine}, it would tip above {altLimit} m/s and would have fallen.
whatIfFail.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine}, tàu sẽ đổ khi vượt {altLimit} m/s, và đã đổ.

whatIfPass.en: With {alt} instead of {mine}, it would stand up to {altLimit} m/s sideways and would have stayed up.
whatIfPass.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine}, tàu đứng vững tới {altLimit} m/s ngang và đã không đổ.

tipTilt.en: Touched down leaning {value}°: past {limit}°, the most this stance (or the flight computer's 20° rule) allows. The ship fell over.
tipTilt.vi: Chạm đất nghiêng {value}°: quá {limit}°, mức tối đa thế đứng này (hoặc giới hạn 20° của máy tính bay) cho phép. Tàu đổ.

legLock.en: One of the {legs} legs did not lock open before touchdown.
legLock.vi: Một trong {legs} chân không khoá mở trước khi chạm đất.

legWeak.en: One leg's shock absorber was weak: the set took {pct} % of its rated energy.
legWeak.vi: Bộ giảm chấn của một chân bị yếu: cả bộ chỉ hấp thụ được {pct} % năng lượng định mức.

chuteOpen.en: Opened at Mach {value}, {altitudeM} m up (rated to Mach {limit}).
chuteOpen.vi: Mở ở Mach {value}, độ cao {altitudeM} m (chịu tới Mach {limit}).

whatIfFail.en: With {alt} instead of {mine} (rated to Mach {altLimit}), it would have torn opening at Mach {value}.
whatIfFail.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine} (chịu tới Mach {altLimit}), dù đã rách khi mở ở Mach {value}.

chuteTorn.en: Fired at Mach {value} {altitudeM} m up, beyond its Mach {limit} limit: the canopy tore.
chuteTorn.vi: Bung ở Mach {value}, độ cao {altitudeM} m, vượt giới hạn Mach {limit}: tán dù bị rách.

whatIfPass.en: With {alt} instead of {mine} (rated to Mach {altLimit}), it would have held.
whatIfPass.vi: Nếu dùng {alt} thay cho {mine} (chịu tới Mach {altLimit}), dù đã không rách.

chuteLostOne.en: One canopy of {canopies} failed to open; the others carried the ship.
chuteLostOne.vi: Một trong {canopies} tán dù không mở; các tán còn lại vẫn đỡ được tàu.

chuteReserve.en: The main canopy failed; the reserve opened with {pct} % of its drag.
chuteReserve.vi: Tán dù chính hỏng; dù dự phòng mở ra với {pct} % lực cản.

power.en: On Mars the power parts gave {value} W averaged over a sol (solar {solarW} W after distance, dust and night; RTG {rtgW} W), with {storeKWh} kWh stored.
power.vi: Trên Sao Hỏa các bộ phận điện cho trung bình {value} W mỗi sol (pin mặt trời {solarW} W sau khoảng cách, bụi và đêm; RTG {rtgW} W), cùng {storeKWh} kWh dự trữ.

roverEnergy.en: The rovers drove {km} km on {value} Wh of battery; the ship charged {chargedWh} Wh back into them (an LRV holds 100 Wh on the surface clock).
roverEnergy.vi: Xe tự hành chạy {km} km, dùng {value} Wh pin; tàu sạc lại cho chúng {chargedWh} Wh (pin LRV chứa 100 Wh theo đồng hồ trên bề mặt).

upload.en: The logs left the ship at {value} bit/s: {waitS} s here, about {realHours} hours in reality (with the wait for the link).
upload.vi: Nhật ký rời tàu ở {value} bit/giây: {waitS} giây trong game, khoảng {realHours} giờ ngoài đời thật (tính cả lúc chờ đường truyền).

uploadMinutes.en: The logs left the ship at {value} bit/s: {waitS} s here, about {realMinutes} minutes in reality (with the wait for the link).
uploadMinutes.vi: Nhật ký rời tàu ở {value} bit/giây: {waitS} giây trong game, khoảng {realMinutes} phút ngoài đời thật (tính cả lúc chờ đường truyền).

uploadDays.en: The logs left the ship at {value} bit/s: {waitS} s here, about {realDays} days in reality.
uploadDays.vi: Nhật ký rời tàu ở {value} bit/giây: {waitS} giây trong game, khoảng {realDays} ngày ngoài đời thật.

antennaDead.en: The antenna failed on Mars: nothing could be sent home.
antennaDead.vi: Ăng-ten hỏng trên Sao Hỏa: không gửi được gì về Trái Đất.

sources.what: Apollo LM landing gear: designed for 10 ft/s (3.05 m/s) vertical and 4 ft/s (1.2 m/s) lateral touchdown, primary struts with crushable aluminium honeycomb and 32 in (0.81 m) of stroke, 37 in (0.94 m) footpads, about 9.4 m between opposite footpads.
sources.source: W. F. Rogers, Apollo Experience Report: Lunar Module Landing Gear Subsystem, NASA TN D-6850 (1972)

sources.what: Falcon 9 landing legs: carbon fibre with an aluminium honeycomb core, helium-piston deployment, about 18 m across when open (≈ 5 core diameters; here 12 m for the 2.5 m game ship).
sources.source: SpaceX Falcon 9 user's guide and vehicle page

sources.what: Falcon 9 / Jason-3 landing (17 January 2016): a leg's lock-out collet did not latch, the stage tipped over on the drone ship and exploded.
sources.source: E. Musk / SpaceX statement, January 2016

sources.what: New Glenn GS1: six landing legs, folded flush on the climb; first landing on the ship Jacklyn on 13 November 2025.
sources.source: Blue Origin (part data in sections/tail/parts.json)

sources.what: New Shepard booster: four short legs deployed just before a powered touchdown at a few m/s.
sources.source: Blue Origin New Shepard flights (2015 onward)

sources.what: Mars Pathfinder airbags: the lander struck Mars at about 18 m/s and bounced some 15 m high; energy per kg of bag here (690 J/kg) is an estimate from that landing.
sources.source: NASA JPL Mars Pathfinder EDL; Cadogan, Sandy & Grahne, Acta Astronautica 50 (2002)

sources.what: Viking lander footpads: wide shallow dishes with crushable rims for loose soil.
sources.source: NASA SP-4212, On Mars: Exploration of the Red Planet (1984)

sources.what: Canopy types: disk-gap-band, ribbon and hemisflo canopies are the supersonic designs; ringsails and flat circular canopies are subsonic mains; ram-air parafoils open only slow.
sources.source: T. W. Knacke, Parachute Recovery Systems Design Manual, NWC TP 6575 (1991)

sources.what: Every Mars lander from Viking to Phoenix opened a disk-gap-band between about Mach 1.1 and 2.1; MSL and Mars 2020 opened theirs at about Mach 1.7.
sources.source: J. R. Cruz & J. S. Lingard, Aerodynamic Decelerators for Planetary Exploration, AIAA 2006-6792

sources.what: Mars 2020 (Perseverance): one 21.5 m disk-gap-band, opened at about Mach 1.75.
sources.source: NASA JPL Mars 2020 EDL

sources.what: Apollo: two conical-ribbon drogues at about 7 km, then three 25.5 m ringsail mains; Apollo 15 landed safely on two when one collapsed (1971).
sources.source: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report (MSC-05161)

sources.what: Soyuz: one main of about 1,000 m² and a reserve of about 574 m², fired by a backup system if the main fails.
sources.source: Soyuz descent module recovery system (RSC Energia)

sources.what: Crew Dragon: two drogues at about 5.5 km, then four mains at about 1.8 km; it lands within limits on three.
sources.source: NASA Demo-2 mission overview (2020)

sources.what: Gemini: one 84 ft (25.6 m) ringsail main, with drogue and pilot chutes, no reserve.
sources.source: NASA Project Gemini familiarization manual

sources.what: X-38: the largest parafoil flown (about 690 m²), deployed slowly after a drogue in drop tests (1999–2001).
sources.source: NASA Dryden X-38 fact sheet

sources.what: Speed of sound near the Martian surface: about 230–240 m/s (CO₂ at 210–240 K).
sources.source: Mars atmosphere data (NASA Mars Fact Sheet; Petculescu & Lueptow, Icarus 186, 2007)

sources.what: Sunlight at Mars' mean distance: 586.2 W/m², 43.1 % of Earth's 1,361 W/m².
sources.source: NASA GSFC Mars Fact Sheet

sources.what: Spirit and Opportunity: about 900 Wh per sol at the start from 1.3 m² of triple-junction cells (rated about 490 W in Earth sunlight), so a sol gives about 4.3 hours at full Mars sunlight: 17.4 % of the day.
sources.source: NASA JPL Mars Exploration Rover power subsystem

sources.what: Dust settling on solar cells at Ares Vallis: 0.28 % of the power lost per sol.
sources.source: G. A. Landis & P. P. Jenkins, J. Geophys. Res. 105 (E1), 1855 (2000)

sources.what: A rocket landing blows dust onto nearby surfaces (Apollo 12 sand-blasted Surveyor 3 from 155 m); airbag landers fire their rockets high above the ground. The 5 % loss on the ship's own panels is an estimate.
sources.source: Immer et al., Icarus 211 (2011); estimate

sources.what: MMRTG (Curiosity, Perseverance): about 110 W of electricity at launch from 2 kW of heat, 45 kg, losing a few per cent a year (107 W assumed after the 8.5-month trip).
sources.source: NASA Radioisotope Power Systems, MMRTG fact sheet

sources.what: Hydrogen + oxygen → water releases 237 kJ/mol of free energy (3.7 kWh per kg of water); a fuel cell turns about 65 % of it into electricity. Reactants left on Mars (44 hours at full power) are an estimate: cryogenic hydrogen boils off on a long trip.
sources.source: Standard Gibbs energy of formation of water; NASA Shuttle fuel cell powerplant

sources.what: Space lithium-ion packs: about 150 Wh/kg (the battery card); they lose about 2 % a month unless kept charged (16 % in 8.5 months).
sources.source: Battery card (sections/body/parts.json); typical Li-ion data, estimate

sources.what: Apollo LRV: two 36 V, 121 Ah silver-zinc batteries (≈ 8.7 kWh). They were primary batteries: activated once and never recharged on the Moon.
sources.source: NASA LRV Operations Handbook (1971)

sources.what: The game's LRV takes a charge from the ship (a rechargeable silver-zinc pack would take about a tenth of its capacity per hour: 870 W). The charge rate is an estimate.
sources.source: estimate (silver-zinc cells charge at about C/10)

sources.what: Curiosity's high-gain antenna sends about 160 bit/s straight to a 34 m Deep Space Network dish and 800 bit/s to a 70 m one; omni antennas manage tens of bit/s from Mars.
sources.source: NASA JPL Mars Science Laboratory, communications with Earth

sources.what: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter: a 3 m dish and a 100 W radio send 0.5–6 Mbit/s home depending on the distance.
sources.source: NASA JPL MRO spacecraft telecommunications

sources.what: Electra UHF relay radios: up to 2 Mbit/s from the surface to an orbiter overhead, which stores the data and sends it home. The smallsat's relay radio: 1 Mbit/s (estimate). This is the hop the game times.
sources.source: NASA JPL Electra proximity link payload (MRO, MAVEN)

sources.what: MarCO (2018): the cubesats relayed InSight's landing home at about 8 kbit/s. A smallsat's own link home is that slow, so it forwards the logs over the next hours, after they have left the ship.
sources.source: NASA JPL MarCO mission

sources.what: From Mars, Earth is above the horizon for about half of each sol (24.66 h). A direct link waits for it: starting at a random moment, on average an eighth of a sol (about 3.1 h). Expected value, an estimate.
sources.source: estimate from the sol length (NASA Mars Fact Sheet)

sources.what: A low relay orbiter (about a 2-hour orbit) passes over a site every orbit or two; the expected wait for the next pass is about an hour. Estimate (MRO and Odyssey pass about twice a sol; a dedicated low orbiter more often).
sources.source: estimate; NASA JPL Mars relay network

sources.what: No published number fits this exact case: a defensible choice, stated as an estimate.
sources.source: estimate
